newsitem.title: USA: Divergent U.S. jobs numbers don't faze economists.
newsitem.headline: Divergent U.S. jobs numbers don't faze economists.

text.p: How fast is the U.S. labor market really growing?

Two monthly government surveys that track employment and are released simultaneously -- the establishment and the household surveys -- have shown differing views of labor market growth over the past few months.
By most standards, though, the labor market is doing fine, and far better than almost everyone's expectations going into 1996.
October data were not as divergent as prior months, but the household survey clearly showed a much stronger labor market than the establishment survey, economists said.

"The last two months, there's been a difference of 400,000 (jobs)," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "It's clear that the household survey shows a more vibrant labor market."
In October, the discrepancy was minor as the establishment survey showed a nonfarm payroll rise of 210,000, while job growth was up 259,000 in the household survey.
But September's figures showed a glaring difference, with nonfarm payrolls dropping 35,000, yet the household survey posted a 313,000 job gain.

So while the establishment survey puts job growth at a total of 175,000 the past two months, the household survey puts it at a whopping 572,000. And over the past three months, nonfarm payroll growth averaged 152,000, whereas civilian employment seen in the household survey averaged 248,000.

Jim Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc, said he uses both sets of numbers, but noted that the establishment survey is more reliable, since the household figures are "very volatile." He added, though, that both are needed to get the clearest picture of the labor market.
"The more the better," he said. "But even these two aren't enough. We need to put them together with jobless claims."
He pointed out that while payrolls show momentum in the labor market, the unemployment rate -- part of the household survey -- tells of broader labor trends and whether the market is tight or not.

It's no surprise that the two surveys differ, since they measure separate things. According to the Labor Department, the establishment survey looks at industries and polls some 400,000 firms about how many jobs they have filled, while the household survey interviews more than 50,000 households about their job situations.

Labor said the two surveys tell different things. One staff economist said the household survey gives a better sense of demographics -- items such as age, sex, race, education level -- and those unemployed or not in the labor force, while the establishment poll provides more comprehensive information on job classifications.

Also, the household measure includes agricultural and self-employed workers, while the establishment one doesn't. But if a person holds two jobs, the household survey counts only one of them, whereas all the jobs a person has are counted in the establishment survey.

"You can't look at these numbers on a month-to-month basis and expect a consistent pattern," said Philip Rones, chief of the division of labor force statistics at the Bureau of Labor Statistics. "On a month-to-months basis, they tell you a different story. Sometimes, they are right on; when they do (match), it's more luck than anything."
He added that over the past year, the establishment survey has reported a job gain of 2.5 million people, while the household survey reported a similar 2.4 million gain.

"That's not always the case," Rones said. "On a short-term analysis, it's hard to take the population (household) survey literally. Because of the size of the survey, the data are stretching the statistics' reliability."

John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co Inc, noted that both surveys tend to converge over the long run. He pointed to average payrolls growth of 207,000 over the past 12 months, while the household survey reported a 199,000 average.

Still, the household survey has shown labor force growth of 1.8 million people this year, "greater than projections of 1.3 million people," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Primark Descision Economics. "What's most striking is that everyone has found a job."
Sinai predicted that the household survey would eventually move in line with the establishment survey and its less-robust picture of the labor market.
The establishment survey "was not as strong, but it was good," he said. "All the (October) reports said to me was that the economy and labor market are on a slower growth path.
"We don't have a weak labor market, just softer than what we've seen."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
